title: Clonidine, methyldopa and noradrenaline: lowering or raising sympathetic tone
ariaLabel: Schematic of sympathetic control of vessels: the brainstem sends sympathetic outflow, nerve endings release noradrenaline, and noradrenaline acts on alpha-1 receptors to narrow vessels. Clonidine and methyldopa act on alpha-2 receptors in the brainstem and nerve endings to lower outflow and release, and noradrenaline given as a drug acts on vascular receptors.
caption: Schematic, not to scale. Flow and levels are qualitative and illustrative; no dose, concentration or lipid value is shown or implied.
blockInfo: A drug of the chosen class acting at this step (generic teaching symbol, not a named drug's shape). Less passes here, with the effects shown at the cholesterol and the LDL receptors.

nodes.label: Vessel alpha-1
nodes.info: Alpha-1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle.

nodes.label: Blood pressure
nodes.info: A teaching score for the blood pressure produced by sympathetic tone.

edges.label: alpha-2 (brain)
edges.info: Clonidine acts on alpha-2 receptors in the brainstem; methyldopa is converted to alpha-methylnoradrenaline, which does the same. Outflow falls.

edges.label: alpha-2 (ending)
edges.info: Alpha-2 receptors on nerve endings reduce further release. Clonidine adds to this brake.

edges.label: alpha-1 receptors
edges.info: Noradrenaline given as a drug acts on alpha-1 receptors (and beta-1 in the heart) and raises pressure; it is a first-line pressor in shock.

sources: Where each class acts. Clonidine and methyldopa act on alpha-2 receptors to lower sympathetic outflow and release, and noradrenaline acts on alpha-1 receptors to narrow vessels. This is standard teaching in the pharmacology texts the PrepNucleus lessons cite (Katzung; KD Tripathi) and were not checked against a linked source here, so they are flagged for review.
simplified: Adrenaline, phenylephrine, dopamine and vasopressin as pressors, rebound after stopping clonidine, methyldopa in pregnancy, haemolysis and liver effects, sedation, shock management and dosing are left out. Blood pressure is drawn as a teaching score. Levels and the size of each effect are illustrative. The drug choices are teaching toggles of a class: no named drug, dose or schedule is shown or implied, and the figure does not say who should or should not take any of them.
